lines.text: In August nineteen eighty-six, a lake in Cameroon exhaled.
By morning, one thousand seven hundred and forty-six people were dead.
Almost none of them woke up.
Seven ways the ground you are standing on can kill you.
Ranked by the only thing that actually matters when it happens.
How much warning you get.
One. The lake.
Lake Nyos sits in a volcanic crater in north-west Cameroon.
Magma underneath leaks carbon dioxide into the water, and the weight of the lake above keeps it dissolved.
The lake is a bottle of fizzy water, and it has been filling for centuries.
On the twenty-first of August, something shook it. Probably a landslide.
Between one hundred and three hundred thousand tonnes of carbon dioxide came out of solution at once.
The column left the surface at about a hundred kilometres an hour.
Then it did the thing that killed everyone. Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, so it did not rise. It flowed downhill.
It poured into the valleys, filled the villages like water filling a bath, and displaced every breathable thing in them.
Seventeen hundred and forty-six people. Three and a half thousand cattle. Out to twenty-five kilometres.
Three lakes on Earth are known to be able to do this. Nyos, Monoun, and Kivu.
Kivu is the big one. It is a thousand times the volume, and about two million people live around its shore.
Nyos and Monoun now have pipes running to the bottom, venting them slowly and permanently, so the charge can never build again.
Warning given: none. The first sign was the smell, and by then you were already breathing it.
Two. The flow.
A pyroclastic flow is not lava. Lava you can walk away from.
This is a ground-hugging avalanche of gas, ash and rock that can move at several hundred kilometres an hour.
Faster than a car. Considerably faster than you.
In seventy-nine, Herculaneum was hit by one from Vesuvius.
The clearest example is Martinique, nineteen oh two. Mont Pelee opened sideways and the cloud came down the slope at about a hundred and sixty kilometres an hour.
The flows themselves reached about four hundred and sixty-five degrees.
Saint-Pierre was the largest city on the island. It was destroyed in under a minute, with about thirty thousand people in it.
There were three known survivors. One was in a half-underground solitary cell with one narrow slit in the door, put there the day before for fighting.
The walls built to keep him in were the only thing in the city thick enough to keep the volcano out. He was dug out three days later.
But something arrived ahead of them. A cloud of ash, hotter still, above five hundred and ten.
In a building near the shore, a man was lying on a wooden bed. The heat arrived and left so quickly that part of his brain turned to glass.
Not burnt. Vitrified. Heated past five hundred degrees and cooled again fast enough to set like obsidian.
It is the only confirmed case of human brain tissue turning to glass that anyone has found.
Warning given: seconds. You see it coming down the mountain, and that is all the information you get.
Three. The floor.
Most of Florida is built on limestone, and limestone dissolves in slightly acidic rainwater.
So underneath the lawns there are voids, and the only thing holding the roof of a void up is the sand sitting on it.
In two thousand and thirteen, in a house in Seffner, a man called Jeffrey Bush went to bed.
At about half past eleven at night, the floor of his bedroom opened.
His brother heard it, ran in, and found the room gone. He jumped in after him and had to be pulled out as the edges kept collapsing.
The hole was too unstable to enter. Jeffrey Bush was never recovered.
The house was demolished. The sinkhole has reopened twice since, in the same spot.
Warning given: none. The ground above a void looks exactly like the ground that is not.
Four. The slosh.
A seiche is what happens when a body of water is pushed at exactly its own rhythm, and starts sloshing like a bath.
In seventeen fifty-five, an earthquake destroyed Lisbon.
Two thousand kilometres away, the water in Loch Lomond and Loch Ness stood up and started swinging, in lakes nobody had felt shake.
In two thousand and eleven, the same thing happened in reverse.
The earthquake off Japan sent waves through the inside of the planet, and about thirty minutes later the fjords of Norway began to move.
A metre and a half, trough to peak, for hours. Eight thousand kilometres from the epicentre. Moored boats were torn loose.
And the waves that did it were not the ones that shake buildings. They were body waves, passing underneath.
Warning given: about half an hour, if anyone thinks to tell you that a quake on the far side of the world is relevant to your harbour.
Five. The sun.
On the first of September eighteen fifty-nine, the sun threw a cloud of magnetised plasma directly at us.
Auroras were seen over Cuba and Hawaii. People in the north-eastern United States could read a newspaper outside at one in the morning.
The telegraph network, the only electrical infrastructure on Earth at the time, started behaving strangely.
Operators disconnected their batteries and kept sending messages anyway, running the line on the current the storm was inducing in it.
In some offices the paper caught fire.
In eighteen fifty-nine, that was the entire damage report. Scorched paper and a few burnt relay stations.
The problem is what we have built since.
A storm that size today would push direct current into a grid built for alternating current, saturating the largest transformers until they cook themselves from inside.
Those transformers are custom-built, and there is no warehouse of spares.
The most cited assessment, from a National Research Council report, put recovery at four to ten years, and the cost in trillions.
Warning given: about seventeen hours. This is the one where we would see it leave the sun, and watch it arrive, and it would not help very much.
Six. The one you have been told about.
Seventy-four thousand years ago, Toba, in Sumatra, produced one of the largest eruptions of the last two million years.
Around two and a half thousand cubic kilometres of material. Ash across South Asia, in some places metres deep.
And then the story you have heard. That it nearly finished us. That the human population fell to a few thousand and everyone alive now descends from those survivors.
That part has quietly fallen apart.
Whole-genome sequencing can see population crashes. It does not see one at seventy-four thousand years. The bottlenecks it does find sit at other dates entirely.
And archaeological sites in Africa and India show people carrying on either side of the ash layer, apparently unbothered.
Toba was still an enormous eruption. It just does not appear to have nearly killed us.
And the supervolcano everyone worries about now would be the least sudden death on this list.
Warning given: months. Possibly years. The ground would lift, the earthquakes would swarm, and nobody would be in any doubt.
Seven. The one from outside.
A gamma-ray burst is the most energetic event in the universe. A certain kind of star collapses and fires two narrow beams from its poles.
In a few seconds it releases more energy than our sun will produce in its entire life.
The beams are narrow, which is the only reassuring sentence in this chapter.
If one were pointed at us from a few thousand light years away, the gamma rays would not reach the ground. They would take the ozone layer apart instead.
Then ordinary sunlight does the rest, over the following years, to everything at the bottom of the food chain.
In October twenty twenty-two we were hit by the brightest one ever recorded. It came from a galaxy one point nine billion light years away.
One suggestion is that this is what happened at the end of the Ordovician, four hundred and forty million years ago. It is a hypothesis, not a finding.
From that distance, across that much of the universe, it was still strong enough to measurably disturb the ionosphere of this planet.
Estimates put a burst that bright at about one every ten thousand years. It was not aimed at us properly. It was pointed somewhere near us.
Warning given: none, and not for want of looking. The burst travels at the speed of light. The warning would arrive with it.
So. Ranked by how long you would have.
Supervolcano, months. Solar storm, seventeen hours. Seiche, half an hour. Pyroclastic flow, seconds. Limnic eruption, sinkhole, gamma-ray burst: nothing at all.
Four of the seven give you no useful notice whatsoever.
And the one that gives you the most is the one everybody is frightened of.
The ground is not solid, the air is not reliably breathable, and the sky is not empty. Sleep well.
